extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of the history of advertising; researchers interested in Victorian newspaper practices and matrimonial advertising
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting the standards, practices, and evaluative signals used in Victorian matrimonial advertisements and the matrimonial newspaper (rules, ad content conventions, credibility markers, and agency practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insertion policy / rates
rubrics_metrics.description: 'bona fide notices from ladies and gentlemen desirous of marrying will be inserted at the rate of twelve stamps per forty words,' with a reduction by taking a quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication charging a per-word (per-forty-words) insertion rate; discounts available for bulk purchases. This is presented as one of the front-page 'rules and regulations' the advertiser must comply with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introductions fee condition
rubrics_metrics.description: 'all introductions are given on the understanding that the lady and gentleman shall each pay a fee to the editor within a month after marriage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introductions brokered by the paper carry a post-marriage payment obligation from both parties to the editor — a contractual/service condition of the publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor as intermediary ('address with Editor')
rubrics_metrics.description: Many advertisements state 'Address with Editor' (or similar) so correspondents send replies via the editor rather than directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the editor as an intermediary was standard practice for privacy and control of introductions; the text shows many ads instruct correspondents to address the editor, and the editor would hold/forward cartes-de-visite or correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor offers advice and solicits contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor 'offers ... to give advice on the subject of courtship or marriage' and requests 'contributions calculated to enlighten the public mind in reference to marriage and other kindred subjects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper positioned itself not just as an ad medium but as an advisory organ: it provided courtship/marriage advice and invited prose meant to 'enlighten' readers — an editorial service and content solicitation policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical advertisement content fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements commonly supply age, physical description (height, hair/eye color, looks), occupation or social position, income/fortune, family connections, residence, and preferences for a partner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter reproduces many specimen ads (e.g., 'twenty-three, tall, dark, and good-tempered, and has an income of £500 a year'; 'A Widow ... income £7,000, residing in a handsome house ... would correspond with a Nobleman'). These elements function as the expected information advertisers provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cartes-de-visite / photographs
rubrics_metrics.description: Requesting or enclosing a 'carte-de-visite' (photograph) is a common practice; specimens show 'wish to correspond and receive the carte-de-visite of the favoured one' and 'Photograph and address with Editor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photos were used to indicate personal appearance; the narrative also records cases where cartes-de-visite were misused or returned when suspicions arose, implying a need for caution when sending likenesses to strangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudonyms and grandiose names
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondents frequently adopt pseudonyms — sometimes 'provokingly funny' or 'high-sounding' — taken from favourite heroines or invented titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The use of fanciful pseudonyms is noted as a common stylistic feature of correspondents and can signal literary affectation or affect authenticity assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement as a respectability signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Matrimonial advertisements 'are excluded from the respectable journals of the metropolis' and are commonly found in 'cheap publications' or penny periodicals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The venue that carries the advert functions as a reputational cue: presence in cheaper or specialized matrimonial weeklies indicates a different audience and lower perceived respectability than placement in mainstream respectable journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional / publication-style variation (tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some northern and manufacturing districts ads are 'very matter-of-fact' and business-like; penny periodicals and columns (e.g., London Journal) feature sensational, romantic, or comic answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers and readers should expect stylistic differences by region and publication type — matter-of-fact practical notices versus more romanticized or theatrical notices in cheaper serials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility markers and anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs of inauthenticity or dubious replies include high-flown compositions in disguised hands, profusely scented paper, extravagant claims (e.g., unlikely large fortunes), repeated or boilerplate ads, and very bad spelling/grammar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter gives examples: many replies to a test ad were 'evidently bona fide' except one high-flown, scented letter; servant replies often claimed 'parents eminently respectable' yet showed bad spelling/grammar. These attributes are presented as cues (positive and negative) for assessing the trustworthiness of correspondents and ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of exploitation by agencies and fortune-hunters
rubrics_metrics.description: Matrimonial clubs/agencies exist to secure wives with good fortunes; such arrangements can lead to exploitation, fraud, and unhappy marriages (example: case in Divorce Court where husband sought money and treated wife brutally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats matrimonial agencies and purely financial marriages as practices that can produce cruelty and legal disputes; this functions as a cautionary standard about the risks inherent in commercialized matchmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautionary practice: withhold personal vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative recounts examples where naive frankness (sending a carte or personal details to a stranger) could expose correspondents to danger or conquest by fortune-hunters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit editorial advice: avoid careless disclosure of personal portraits or sensitive information to unknown correspondents; use intermediaries and exercise prudence when replying to adverts.
